source: Nievelstein, van Gog, van Dijck & Boshuizen (2013) The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: learning to reason about legal cases
finding: Design: 2 (worked examples vs solve the cases) x 2 (Toulmin process steps or not) x 2 (first-year novices vs third-year advanced law students). Two learning cases, then one test case on transfer of property. Novices: studying worked examples gave far higher test scores, in about half the learning time.
numbers: First-year (n about 75): test score M=58.63 (SD 27.74) worked examples vs M=8.59 (SD 4.06) problem solving, F(1,68)=105.22, p<.001, Cohen's f=1.24. Learning time 568 s vs 1146 s (f=0.75). Learning effort 5.46 vs 6.39 on a 9-point scale (f=0.42). Test score max 100.
limits: Short single session, only two learning cases, one test case with the same legal rules as the learning cases (no new-rule transfer test), small cells (9 per cell for third-year). Scoring by one rater after ICC .87 on 10% of data.
agent_relevance: A less structured, rule-application task still gained a very large benefit from a worked solution. Worked cases are not limited to closed-form tasks when the rules are known and the answer can be checked by a rubric.

source: Nievelstein et al. (2013) third-year students: no expertise reversal
finding: Third-year students had much more prior knowledge, did better and worked with less effort than first-years, yet worked examples still beat problem solving. No expertise reversal appeared. The authors say less structured tasks take longer to master, so examples stay useful longer.
numbers: Third-year (n=9 per cell, 36 total): test M=82.28 (SD 18.11) worked examples vs M=37.06 (SD 26.71) problem solving, F(1,32)=37.03, p<.001, f=1.02. Learning time 427 s vs 976 s, f=1.00. Prior knowledge test (max 34): third-year 17.12 vs first-year 8.86, d=2.75. Learning effort difference not significant (F(1,32)=2.22, p=.15).
quote: an expertise reversal effect did not occur
limits: Authors cannot tell whether examples helped by teaching the specific law or by improving reasoning. Small n. The advanced group are still only third-year students, not practising lawyers.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that a stronger model or a more familiar task removes the benefit of showing worked cases in less structured work. Expertise reversal may be weaker when tasks are open. Test it, do not assume it.

source: Nievelstein et al. (2013) process steps alone (Toulmin argument model)
finding: Giving novices only the five generic reasoning steps (grounds, warrants, backings, rebuttals, qualifier, conclusion) without worked-out solutions did not help learning but made them slower. Abstract guidance without solved cases is a weak support for open tasks.
numbers: First-year, problem solving with steps vs without: time 1460.72 s (SD 459.41) vs 831.58 s (SD 337.64), t(34)=4.68, d=1.56. Test score about 8.33 vs 8.88 (no difference, main effect of process steps F(1,68)<1). Effort 6.92 vs 5.86 with steps.
limits: Novices only for this conclusion. The authors suggest steps might suit advanced students, but third-year data showed no step effect either (F(1,32)<1).
agent_relevance: A checklist of general steps in the open mode (a schema without exemplars) may cost tokens and not improve results. Pair any step list with at least one worked case, or measure first.

source: Renkl (2023) Using worked examples for ill-structured learning content (chapter, In Their Own Words, APA Division 2)
finding: Defines ill-structured learning content as content with no algorithm that guarantees a solution: only heuristics. Says the worked-example effect was first shown for well-structured content and has since been tried for argumentation, proof finding, concept mapping, negotiation, essay and literature writing, design styles and teachers' professional vision. Argues the same load explanation applies: learners who are overwhelmed copy surface patterns.
numbers: No pooled effect size given. Lists studies (Hefter 2014/2018/2019, Schworm and Renkl 2007, Hilbert 2008, Reiss 2008, Martin 2022, Nievelstein 2013, Kyun 2013, Rourke and Sweller 2009).
limits: Narrative chapter by a leading proponent. No count of failures. Notes the studies are mostly 'kick-off interventions' for skills that need longer training.
agent_relevance: Gives a design rule for open mode: teach the heuristics first, then show worked cases, then ask for self-explanation. It reframes 'open' tasks as heuristic tasks, not as a different kind of reasoning.

source: Renkl (2023) two content levels: learning domain vs exemplifying domain
finding: Examples for ill-structured content carry two levels: the skill to be learned (e.g. how to build an argument) and the topic used to show it (e.g. lynx in a forest). Learners must process both. Low prior knowledge of the topic gave poor learning of the skill. Prompts that pointed at the topic instead of the skill hurt learning of the skill. Fill-in gaps in the geometry hurt learning to prove.
numbers: Cites Hilbert et al. (2004, 2008) for low topic knowledge and Schworm and Renkl (2007) for prompts aimed at the example topic. No effect sizes given in the chapter.
quote: comprehension difficulties in the exemplifying domain can hinder learners from seeing how the learning domain's principles are instantiated
limits: Effect sizes for these two boundary findings are in the original papers, which were not opened.
agent_relevance: When the agent shows itself a past case for an open task, the case's subject matter can distract from the reasoning pattern. Store cases with the pattern labelled, keep the topic simple, and prompt on the pattern.

source: Renkl (2023) video vs text vs graphic novel examples; segmentation of video examples
finding: Hefter et al. (2019): video argumentation examples gave no learning advantage over text or graphic-novel versions, but text and graphic novels took less time. Martin et al. (2022): in a 90-minute seminar, student teachers noticed and interpreted best with segmented videos (3-4 min) plus pre-structured self-explanation prompts, but did not transfer this to new unsegmented videos without prompts.
numbers: No numbers given in the chapter. Videos 7-10 min cut to 3-4 min segments.
limits: Second-hand report. Single-session interventions; transfer failed to unsupported conditions.
agent_relevance: Support for open tasks may be tool-bound: skill shown under scaffolding may not carry over when the scaffold is removed. The agent's open mode should keep the scaffold on, not assume it was learned.

source: Bichler, Stadler, Bühner, Greiff & Fischer (2022) Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect? Instructional Science 50
finding: Re-analysis of Schwaighofer et al. (2016) data. 74 university students self-explained while studying worked examples or solving ill-defined statistics problems (no algorithmic solution). Self-explanation quality did not mediate any worked example effect. The shifting and fluid-intelligence interactions from the original study were reproduced. Working memory capacity did not moderate the effect.
numbers: N=74. Worked example effect on self-explanation quality b=1.78, one-tailed p=.234, CI [-2.58, 5.38]; indirect effect b=0.14, CI [-0.03, 0.42]; direct effect on post-test b=0.65, p=.120. Self-explanation quality (0-24.5 scale): worked examples M=13.56 vs problem solving M=11.67. Quality correlated with post-test r=.37 (p=.001) but not with gain r=.16. Prior knowledge did not moderate the direct effect (b=-0.02).
limits: The abstract and text show the worked-example advantage on gains is weaker than for algebra-type tasks, and the mediation is null. Single lab, university students, data shared with the earlier paper (not an independent sample).
agent_relevance: In ill-defined problems the example works as a strategy to copy, not by raising explanation quality. Do not count on self-explanation prompts as the active ingredient. Check the effect on pass rate, not on explanation quality.

source: Bichler et al. (2022) / Schwaighofer et al. (2016) / Bichler et al. (2020): individual differences that moderate the effect in ill-defined tasks
finding: Worked examples helped learners with weaker shifting ability more, and the benefit shrank as shifting ability and fluid intelligence rose. This pattern was found in the first study and replicated once (Bichler 2020, as reported). Working memory capacity did not moderate it, which favours the cognitive load claim that capacity limits apply to everyone in complex learning.
numbers: Replication of the two interaction effects confirmed in the text. Exact coefficients for the shifting and Gf interactions were not extracted from the pages read.
limits: Reported second-hand from the 2022 paper for the 2016 and 2020 studies. Higher-ability learners showed a smaller benefit, not a reversal.
agent_relevance: The moderator that matters is flexible switching between approaches, not raw capacity. A strong model can switch strategies itself and may need fewer cases on open tasks; a weak one needs more.

source: Chen thesis (2015, UNSW) via Chen, Kalyuga & Sweller: Kyun, Kalyuga & Sweller (2013) English literature essays, as described in Chen's thesis
finding: Three experiments with Korean students (English as a foreign language) writing essays on English literature. The worked example advantage appeared only as learner knowledge fell. Most experienced group: no difference on retention, near or far transfer. Middle group: worked examples better on retention only. Least knowledgeable group: better on retention and marginally better on near and far transfer.
numbers: Description only. Secondary sources found by search describe 63 and 62 female university students in Experiments 1 and 2 and scoring with IELTS writing rubrics. No test statistics were read.
limits: Second-hand description from a thesis; the original (J Exp Educ 81, 385-408) was not opened. The authors suggest a factorial design and more consistent scoring in future work.
agent_relevance: For a writing task the example effect behaves like a classic expertise reversal. The better the learner, the less examples help. Open-mode cases should be gated by how weak the agent is on that task class.

source: Chen thesis (2015) via Rourke & Sweller (2009) The worked-example effect using ill-defined problems: learning to recognise designers' styles
finding: As described in the thesis: students learning design history studied worked examples with paired problems, or solved problems only. A worked-example effect appeared, but on both near and far transfer only for participants who already had some domain-specific knowledge. This is the reverse of a simple 'novice only' rule: ill-defined recognition needs some base before examples pay off.
numbers: No statistics in the secondary text. Three stages: lecture, example or practice stage, test stage.
quote: only participants with domain-specific knowledge demonstrated the worked example effect for both near and far transfer tests
limits: The original paper was not opened (only a thesis paraphrase and a search snippet confirming the citation: Learning and Instruction 19, 185-199).
agent_relevance: Worked cases in an open task need a minimum of vocabulary and categories to attach to. A cold-start agent with no prior in the area may not benefit; give a short primer first.

source: Chen thesis (2015, UNSW) Worked example effect, generation effect and element interactivity
finding: Resolves the apparent clash between the worked example effect and the generation effect: materials low in element interactivity favour self-generation, high element interactivity favours worked examples. Experiment 1 (grade 4, geometry) found a disordinal interaction of guidance by element interactivity. Experiments 2 and 3 used older students; the interaction was predicted to shrink with expertise.
numbers: Three experiments with grade 4, 6 and 7 students; two 35-minute phases (generation phase and worked example phase). Exact test statistics were not extracted.
limits: A thesis; the interaction was the prediction under test and was stated as confirmed for Experiment 1. Experiments 2 and 3 results were not read. Element interactivity is set by the author, not measured independently.
agent_relevance: The task-type rule is about how many interacting elements must be held together, not about 'open vs closed'. Open tasks with many interacting parts should still gain from cases; open tasks that are really recall-and-fill should not.

source: Chen thesis (2015) review of worked examples in ill-structured domains: Owens & Sweller (2008) music; Hübner, Nückles & Renkl (2010)
finding: Thesis review states: research in music (Owens & Sweller 2008), design history (Rourke & Sweller 2009) and social psychology (Hübner et al. 2010) shows an effect in less structured domains; the format must still give an expert solution. In music, integrating text with notation (to avoid split attention) produced the worked example effect in both a text-and-notation and an audio experiment.
numbers: None given.
limits: Second-hand and written by a Sweller-group student. Says 'much less research' exists in ill-structured domains than in well-structured ones, so absence of failures is partly absence of studies.
agent_relevance: Count of studies for open tasks is small and all from related groups. Treat 'effect found in open tasks' as supported but thin, with a publication-bias risk.

source: Van Gog & Rummel (2010) Example-based learning: integrating cognitive and social-cognitive research perspectives, Educational Psychology Review 22
finding: Review notes that worked examples first came from algebra, geometry and physics, and have more recently been used for less structured skills such as writing and argumentation, with legal reasoning (Nievelstein et al., then a manuscript) and design styles (Rourke and Sweller 2009) cited. Its summary table lists 'less structured problems/tasks' as a learner and task variable.
numbers: No pooled numbers for the task-type moderator.
limits: Only text matching 'ill-structured' and 'less structured' was read in this session, not the whole review. No effect-size comparison across task structure.
agent_relevance: Confirms that, as of 2010, task structure was an open moderator with few studies. A third-party review did not quantify it.

source: Marsh, Landau & Hicks (1996) How examples may (and may not) constrain creativity, Memory & Cognition 24, 669-680
finding: Three experiments tested the claim of Smith, Ward and Schumacher (1993) that creative ideas conform to shown examples. Conformity was found in all three: people copied critical features of examples. But total output, elaborateness and non-critical features did not show that creativity was reduced. More examples increased conformity (Exp 1). A delay raised conformity (Exp 3).
numbers: Exp 1 (80 participants, about 16 per group, 0-9 examples): share of critical features rose from 4.4% (no examples, 6.6 features per creation) to 12.1% (nine examples, 7.1 features), omnibus F(4,75)=4.15, p<.01. Exp 3 delay: conformity score rose, F(1,73)=4.74, p<.05; number of creations and features did not change (F<1).
limits: Creature-drawing task (inventing alien animals). Feature copying was measured by the experimenters, creativity by ratings in Exp 2 only. Exp 2 found that examples with unnatural feature pairs were rated more creative.
agent_relevance: Shown cases leak into open-ended output, more with more cases and with a gap in time. Copying does not always lower overall output quantity or rated creativity. Use few diverse cases and measure the output for copying.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso (2024) The effects of generative AI on design fixation and divergent thinking, CHI '24
finding: Between-participants experiment (N=60; 20 per condition: no support, image search, AI image generator) with a 20-minute avatar sketching task that began with an example. AI image support produced more fixation on the example, fewer ideas, less variety and lower originality than the baseline.
numbers: Design fixation (share of 14 example features): GenAI estimate +0.32 (89% CI [0.11, 0.54]), Bayes factor 124; image search +0.27 (CI [0.05, 0.48]). Fluency (ideas) for GenAI: total-effect estimate -0.21. NASA-TLX overall not different, F(2,57)=1, p=.37.
limits: Humans using a picture generator, not an LLM reasoning. Bayesian models with 89% intervals; small cells; visual design task; baseline condition was the lowest-fixation arm.
agent_relevance: Showing the model ready-made examples in an open creative task anchors the result and cuts the number of distinct ideas. Support this by generating first, then looking at examples.

source: Li, Tang, Chen, Wang, Chen & Abram (2024) Why does in-context learning fail sometimes? Evaluating in-context learning on open and closed questions, arXiv 2407.02028
finding: With GPT-4, the more similar the context was to the question, the more it helped on two closed-form benchmarks (MetaICL, NephSAP). On a new set of open-form hard physics and computer science questions the sign flipped: lower-similarity context gave larger gains, and high-similarity context could hurt.
numbers: Novel dataset: 160 question-response pairs, four context types including no-context control, graded by several graders. Closed-form: positive correlation of similarity with mean score gain; open-form: negative correlation. Effect is stronger for novel and difficult questions. No single effect size read.
quote: the relationship between context-similarity and performance improvement is completely reversed
limits: One model (GPT-4), one small open-form set, graded by humans (grader agreement not read). Preprint, unreviewed. Context = retrieved text, not worked solutions.
agent_relevance: The retrieval rule 'most similar case first' that works for closed tasks may be wrong for open tasks. In open mode retrieve diverse or analogical cases, and test both sorting rules.

source: Upasani, Wu, Rainton, Li, Thakker, Hu & Zhang (2026) Test-time adaptation via many-shot prompting: benefits, limits, and pitfalls, ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2603.05829)
finding: With Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.3-70B Instruct, many-shot demonstrations help most on structure-heavy tasks with constrained outputs (information extraction, reading comprehension) and give small, steady gains on open-ended generation (machine translation). Gains saturate and shuffling order changes accuracy by 2-3 points.
numbers: Banking77: accuracy varies 2-3% across 10 random orders. Reinforced ICL on GPQA Diamond (70B): gains up to 4 reasoning demonstrations then plateau and drop. Table 5 (parsing scrambled): extraction tasks rise from about 40 to about 87-96 with 4 shots; MT gains stay small, e.g. 44.76 to 47.0 on one direction.
quote: limited benefits for open-ended generation tasks
limits: Open-ended tasks tested here were machine translation, which is open-ended but has a reference; no creative or planning tasks. Table 5 text lost its row labels in extraction, so row-to-number mapping is inferred. Authors call findings preliminary.
agent_relevance: The number of cases in context should not be grown on open tasks. Moderate, diverse sets saturate early; for open mode spend tokens on structure and checks, not extra examples.

source: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald & Durrett (2025) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning, ICLR 2025
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. Chain-of-thought (worked reasoning written out) gives large gains on symbolic, math and logic tasks and about nothing elsewhere. On MMLU, gains are almost entirely on items containing an equals sign.
numbers: Mean gains: symbolic +14.2, math +12.3, logical +6.9. Those three categories: 56.9 with CoT vs 45.5 without. All other categories: 56.8 vs 56.1.
quote: CoT gives strong performance benefits primarily on tasks involving math or logic
limits: Compares CoT with direct answer, not with other scaffolds; compute not matched (authors say the small gain elsewhere is not a win for CoT). Task labels come from the paper categories.
agent_relevance: Closest large-scale LLM analogue to the task-type limit: written step-by-step reasoning pays on structured symbolic tasks, not on open ones. Open mode should not default to long reasoning.

source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo & Griffiths (2025) Mind your step (by step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse, ICML 2025 (arXiv 2410.21333)
finding: Six tasks where deliberation hurts people. In three, models did worse with CoT: implicit statistical learning, face recognition, learning labels with exceptions. In artificial grammar classification, CoT cut accuracy in most models.
numbers: Artificial grammar: o1-preview 36.3 points below GPT-4o on a 440-problem subset (94.0% zero-shot GPT-4o vs 57.7% o1-preview). Full set: GPT-4o 87.5% to 64.4% with CoT (-23.1), Claude 3 Opus 70.7 to 62.7 (-8.0), Llama 3.1 70B 65.9 to 57.1 (-8.8); Claude 3.5 Sonnet 65.9 to 67.7 (+1.8, p=.969, not significant). Random = 50%.
limits: Synthetic tasks built from psychology experiments; o1 compared to GPT-4o since its reasoning cannot be turned off; other three tasks gave mixed results.
agent_relevance: Supports a gate before long reasoning or worked traces: some task types get worse when the model talks itself through them. Run the task-type check before enabling slow mode.

source: Yun, An, Wang, Peng & Shang (2025) The price of format: diversity collapse in LLMs, arXiv 2505.18949
finding: Chat-template tokens make instruction-tuned models give similar outputs to open-ended inputs, even at high temperature. Minimal formatting gave the most diverse outputs. Format consistency matters for structured tasks (GSM8K, IFEval) but little for knowledge-heavy ones.
numbers: Demonstration: 1024 news headlines from 'generate a random news'. Plain prompt spread across sports, health, politics; template prompt produced mostly Science. Exact diversity scores not extracted.
limits: Tested on Llama-family models and a few tasks; fine-tuning comparison mixes several factors.
agent_relevance: The scaffold's own wrapper and format can narrow open-ended output. For open mode keep the wrapper light and sample from several framings.

source: Wenger & Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs, arXiv 2501.19361
finding: Humans and many LLMs answered standard creativity tests (Alternate Uses, Forward Flow, Divergent Association). LLMs slightly beat humans on Alternate Uses and Divergent Association; humans slightly beat LLMs on Forward Flow. But LLM answers were much more similar to each other than human answers were to each other, even after controls.
numbers: Effect sizes for individual originality were small; similarity measured as cosine distance of embedded responses. Per-test statistics not copied.
quote: LLM responses are much more similar to other LLM responses than human responses are to each other
limits: Tests are short word tasks, not real design or planning. Embedding-based diversity.
agent_relevance: One model sampled many times is not a diverse search for open tasks. Different models or different framings are needed to get coverage.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan & Anderson (2025) Human creativity in the age of LLMs: randomized experiments on divergent and convergent thinking, CHI '25
finding: Two pre-registered experiments, 1,100 participants. Standard LLM help (direct ideas) or coach-like guidance (strategies) raised assisted creative performance but unassisted performance afterwards was no better and often a bit worse than for people who never had help. Strategy-style guidance led to lasting loss of idea diversity after the tool was removed; direct ideas did not.
numbers: N=1,100 across two experiments (divergent: Alternate Uses; convergent: Remote Associates). Unassisted performance higher for no-exposure group on average, not significant in all cases.
limits: Human outcomes, not LLM outcomes; short single sessions; some contrasts not significant.
agent_relevance: A direct analogue: a given strategy framework may narrow later open thinking. If the scaffold supplies a strategy list, add variation so later passes do not all follow it.

source: Hefter et al. (2019) / Schworm & Renkl (2007) video vs text argumentation examples, as reported in Renkl (2023)
finding: Reported only second-hand: self-explanation prompts on examples of two-sided argumentation improved learning of the argument steps, and prompts aimed at the topic rather than the steps hampered it.
numbers: No numbers available from the sources opened.
limits: Originals not opened; cited only through Renkl (2023).
agent_relevance: Marked as a lead to open next. Do not rely on its numbers.

source: Kyun, Kalyuga & Sweller (2013) The effect of worked examples when learning to write essays in English literature, J Exp Educ 81, 385-408 (search snippet)
finding: Search summary: worked examples helped Korean university students writing essays on children's English literature; the benefit rose as knowledge fell. Answers scored by lecturers with IELTS academic writing rubrics. Authors call for factorial design, more diverse sample and consistent scoring.
numbers: Search summary reports 63 and 62 female students in Experiments 1 and 2; not verified in the paper.
limits: Search snippet only; paper not opened. Single-sex, single-country sample; scoring by lecturers.
agent_relevance: Same as b09: examples help writing most when the learner is weak. Treat counts as unverified.

source: Searches for failed replications of the less-structured-task result (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv searches this session)
finding: No direct replication or failed replication of Nievelstein et al. (2013) was found. OpenAlex quota ran out mid-session and Semantic Scholar rate-limited. Related later work found: Bichler et al. (2022) on ill-defined statistics, and a 2023 Educational Psychology paper on worked examples and solution steps (not opened). A search for LLM studies that test worked examples on ill-structured tasks returned none.
numbers: 0 direct replications found; 0 LLM studies with worked examples in ill-structured tasks found.
limits: Negative search result under quota limits; absence in this search is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: The open-mode claim has no LLM test. Any gain from cases in open mode is an untested prediction for our agent.

source: Li et al. (2024) arXiv 2407.02028: difficulty and novelty as moderators
finding: The reversal for open-form questions was especially visible on high-difficulty and high-novelty questions. This suggests that the harm of too-similar context grows when the model cannot rely on remembered patterns.
numbers: Not quantified in the pages read; reported in abstract and discussion as 'especially visible'.
quote: especially visible for open questions and questions of high difficulty or novelty
limits: Dataset small (160 pairs); no per-model breakdown; GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Condition any case injection on novelty of the task. For tasks outside the library, similar-case retrieval is the wrong default.

source: Upasani et al. (2026) update policy and order effects
finding: Similarity-based example selection is strong early and degrades as more examples are added, while random (diverse) selection scales better. Larger model (70B) benefits earlier and drops at the largest update. Adding cross-label examples beat forcing per-label balance.
numbers: Banking77 (77 classes): best setting n=1 per class with cross-label similarity (N=77 demos). Prompt reaches 128k token limit at n=70 (N=5390 demos). Reinforced ICL context reaches about 14.7k tokens at 32 shots.
quote: relevance helps early, diversity helps at scale
limits: One classification benchmark for selection results; authors say findings are preliminary.
agent_relevance: Support for mixing relevance with diversity as the library grows, and for a hard cap on cases shown.

source: Kumar et al. (2025) strategies vs direct ideas: homogenization persistence
finding: Participants given LLM-generated strategies showed reduced diversity in their idea sets both during and after the tool; participants given direct ideas did not show the same lasting loss once the LLM was gone.
numbers: Directional result from the discussion text; test statistics not copied.
limits: Discussion reading, not table values. Single task family.
agent_relevance: Shared scaffolds can shape later thinking more than shared outputs. Rotate or randomise which strategy prompt is used across attempts in open mode.
